outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text:

---

As phantoms direct life from the shadows, I feel I leaned on something, and it broke. My father, on the porch with his crosswords, said, *this must be what it feels like to be dead.* When I returned from the dead there was no one to greet me, and yet you are glad—I wander the ruins the way my tongue wanders my missing teeth, the bricks and mortar of Deep Deuce rotted like molars in an ancient mouth. Here, Charlie Christian might once have walked—

The astrologer counseled patience and creative visualization:

**Step One:** Visualize an object that symbolizes the accursed influence. Picture yourself casting it into a furnace.

**Step Two:** Visualize the person responsible for the curse. Imagine one end of a rope tied around your waist and the other around that person. Picture yourself severing the rope with a chainsaw as you call out, *"You have no power over me!"*

**Step Three:** Repeat twice a day for eleven days . . .

You visualize her green boots within the furnace . . . —No. You are in a crematorium, and you see her perfect and corruptible body on a tray, sliding into the fire. Then you see yourself cutting the rope that binds you together with a saw. And then, at last, your own imperfect and corruptible body—I mean, *me*—calls out, and I leap in after her.

---

I preserved the poem's imagery, emotional arc, and voice while refining the punctuation, smoothing transitions, and clarifying the formatting of the astrologer's instructions. Let me know if you'd prefer a version that stays even closer to the original line breaks or one that leans further toward formal prose.

Seated on the porch with his crossword puzzles, my father remarked that this was surely how death must feel; Upon coming back from death's territory, not a soul was there to welcome me, yet you remain pleased— I roam through the wreckage just as my tongue explores the gaps where teeth once were, the brickwork of Deep Deuce decayed like molars in some ancient jaw; Charlie Christian may once have strolled through here—

The stargazer advised me to be patient and to practice creative visualization: First, conjure an image of some object that represents the cursed force. See yourself hurling it into flames. Second, envision the individual behind the curse. Imagine a rope with one end knotted at your waist and the other fastened to them. Watch yourself sever that rope with a chainsaw while shouting, "You hold no power over me!" Third, do this two times daily across eleven days . . .

You conjure her green boots within the flames . . . —No. You stand inside a crematorium, watching her flawless yet perishable form on a tray glide toward the fire; Next you observe yourself severing the rope binding the two of you with a saw; And finally your own flawed and perishable form—that is, me—cries out, and I leap in to follow her.
outputs.L3:
# The Severing

Something broke inside me the way a rope breaks under too much weight—suddenly, completely, with a snap I felt more than heard. It was a death, though nothing died that I could bury. One moment I was carrying the certainty of some thing I had leaned my whole life against, and the next that thing was simply gone, and I was falling through the space where it used to be. Loss has a texture. I ran my fingers over the empty places and found them raw.

I wandered into Deep Deuce because a man in mourning wanders, and because the neighborhood was mourning too. The buildings had been left to rot, and their brick facades had begun to crumble in a way that struck me, standing there in the dying light, as almost anatomical. The gaps in the masonry were like the gaps in an old man's smile—here a tooth missing, there one blackened and half-decayed, the whole ancient mouth of the street slowly losing its capacity to speak. I walked past the ruins and felt them recognizing me. We were the same, the buildings and I: structures that had once held something and now held only the memory of holding.

It was the astrologer who gave me a way forward, or claimed to. She read the accursed influence in my chart the way one reads weather, and she prescribed a ritual against it—a working of pure imagination, creative visualization meant to break the curse and sever the cord binding me to the one who had laid it. There was a person responsible, she insisted. There is always a person. And to free myself I had only to see the severing clearly enough in my mind.

The steps were precise. First, I was to picture a symbolic object—the vessel of the curse, its physical anchor in the world—and I was to destroy it utterly, imagine it shattering, burning, dissolving to nothing. Then I was to see the rope itself, the thick cord that ran from my body to hers, and I was to take a blade to it and cut, watching the strands part one by one until nothing connected us. And finally, with the rope severed and the object destroyed, I was to speak the words of independence aloud: *I am free of you. I am beyond your power. You hold nothing of mine.*

I did as I was told. I closed my eyes and I built the images faithfully, and everything proceeded as she had described—until the very end, when the ritual turned in my hands like a living thing and became something else entirely. For at the moment I was meant to declare my freedom, I saw instead her body. I saw it laid out and sliding slowly forward on its track, sliding toward the open mouth of the crematorium, into the fire that waited there. And I did not speak the words. I did not sever anything. I watched her body slide into the flames, and then—God help me, and against every instruction—I jumped in after her.

Some ropes are not meant to be cut. Some cords a man would rather burn beside than survive.
outputs.L4:
**The Accursed Influence**

*I.*

They said you would return in the smell of wet ash,
in the low hour when the lamps gutter and lean,
and you did—
you always did.
I found your fingerprints pressed into the fog,
your absence wearing the shape of every doorway.
The house has learned to breathe without you
but I have not,
and the flowers I set at your photograph
turn brown by morning,
as if grief were something the petals could catch.

*II.*

There is a decay that has no odor,
only weight.
It settles in the marrow, in the hinge of the jaw,
in the way I have forgotten how to swallow.
The mirrors keep your reflection
long after I have left the room.
The bedsheets keep the crease of a body
that is no longer permitted to lie down.

*III.*

So they brought the astrologer,
old as the almanac he carried,
his eyes two coins pressed flat by centuries.
He read the charts of my ruin
and named it plainly:
*an accursed influence, a thread
tied from your wrist to hers,
from the living to the burned.*
*Cut it,* he said,
*and you will walk again among the breathing.*

He gave me salt to scatter,
a knife blessed in cold water,
words to speak against the dark—
a ritual to sever,
a rope to burn at both its ends,
an exorcism dressed as mercy.

*IV.*

I carried these instructions to the ghat,
where the pyre was already speaking its orange language,
where the smoke climbed like a prayer
that had given up on heaven.
I held the knife.
I held the salt.
I held every reason I was given
to remain.

*V.*

But love is not a thread to be cut—
it is a gravity,
a direction the whole body obeys.
When the flames took the last of you,
I understood the astrologer had misread the sky:
the accursed influence was never a curse,
it was the only true north I had left.

So I let the salt fall from my open hand.
I let the blessed knife lie useless in the ash.
And I stepped forward—
not to sever,
but to follow,
into the fire that was already learning your name,
into the one embrace
that no ritual could undo.

They wanted to teach me how to survive you.
I chose instead to keep you,
even at the cost of the keeper.

# The Tension of Deuce

There is no moment in tennis quite like reaching **deuce**. When the score locks at 40-40, the entire rhythm of the match shifts. Suddenly, every point carries the weight of the whole game, and players must dig deep into their reserves of focus and skill.

**When** a match arrives at deuce, momentum can swing wildly in either direction. One player might feel the pressure mounting, while the other senses an opportunity to seize control. The crowd falls silent, sensing that the next few exchanges could decide everything. It is in these moments that champions separate themselves from the rest.

To survive deuce, a player often relies on going **deep**. A deep serve pushes the opponent back behind the baseline, robbing them of angles and time. Deep groundstrokes keep the pressure relentless, forcing errors from an opponent who has no room to attack. Playing deep is not just about power—it is about strategy, patience, and precision under stress.

The beauty of deuce lies in its endlessness. A single game can stretch through advantage after advantage, each side clawing back to level. When neither player will yield, the battle becomes as much mental as physical. Every deep shot, every calculated risk, brings them one step closer to breaking the deadlock.

In the end, deuce reminds us why tennis is such a thrilling sport. When the stakes are highest and both competitors refuse to break, we witness the deep resolve that defines true athletes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem that weaves together grief, a curse-removal ritual with visualization steps, and imagery of Deep Deuce and Charlie Christian.
counterfactuals.output:
# Second Line for a Ghost in the Amplifier

They told me grief was a curse you could unstitch if you knew the ritual, so here in the blue hour I gather what the instructions ask for: a bowl of tap water, a candle the color of a trumpet's throat, and the memory of your hands.

*Step one: name what you are carrying.* I name it. It has your face and the weight of a piano no one moved from the church basement.

*Step two: close your eyes and see the street where it began.* And there it is—Deep Deuce, Second and Central, the bricks still warm from a summer that ended before I was born. The Aldridge marquee spelling out a night that will not come again. I walk it the way you taught me to walk anything: slow, listening for the downbeat under my shoes.

*Step three: find the light and let it move through you.* So I find Charlie Christian on the corner, seventeen and electric, the first man to make a guitar speak in a voice loud enough to argue with the dead. His amplifier hums like a hive of small forgivenesses. He is playing something that has no name yet, something that will not have a name until after he is gone—consumption taking him at twenty-five, the way it takes the brightest first, the way it took you, the way it takes everyone who learns to bend a note until it cries.

*Step four: visualize the curse leaving your body as smoke.* But grief is not smoke. Grief is a solo that keeps quoting itself. It is Charlie's single-string melody climbing over the rhythm section of my ribs, and I cannot tell if I am being emptied or filled.

*Step five: submerge your hands in the water and release.* I do. The candle throws your shadow on the wall, then throws his, then throws the whole vanished district—the drugstore, the barbershop, the hall where the horns leaned out the windows like men in love. All of it dredged up by the freeway years ago, all of it living now only in the low frequency I can't stop humming.

Here is what the ritual didn't say: some curses are just love with nowhere left to land. Some hauntings are a kindness. When I lift my hands, the water holds the ceiling's small flame like a note held past the count, and I understand I will not be cured of you.

So let the last step be this: I leave the candle burning. I leave Deep Deuce lit inside me like a club that never closed. I let Charlie play us both out—the boy, the district, the you-shaped silence—down the long amplified dark, where nothing is removed, only carried, only kept, only played again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece blending fragments about death, a father doing crosswords, missing teeth, and an astrologer's three-step ritual for breaking a curse.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Astrologer's Instructions, Interrupted

*

Step one: you must gather what has fallen from your body. She said this without looking up. The teeth first, if you have them. Most people, she said, do not keep their teeth.

*

My father fills in FOUR ACROSS. A five-letter word for *ending*. He does not say the word aloud. He writes it in small capitals, the way he writes everything, as if permanence were a matter of penmanship.

*

I had three molars pulled the winter my mother— The dentist offered them to me in a small envelope, the kind that holds a single button. I threw them away. I did not know I would need them.

*

Step two, the astrologer said. You will burn something that remembers you.

What remembers me?

She shrugged. A photograph. A coat. A tooth would have been ideal, but you've told me about the teeth.

*

SIX DOWN: what the dead leave (7 letters). My father taps the pen against the crossword. *Absence* has seven letters. So does *silence*. So does *nothing*, if you count wrong, which grief teaches you to do.

*

Here is the thing about a curse: it is only a story insisting on being finished.

*

When my mother died my father did not weep at first. He did the crossword. He did the crossword every morning for a year, the way a man might touch a wall in the dark to know which room he is standing in. Kitchen. Hallway. The room where she is not.

*

Step three. The astrologer folded her hands. This is the hardest. You must speak to the one who cursed you and thank them.

But I don't know who cursed me.

Then you must thank everyone. Slowly. One at a time. It will take the rest of your life.

Yes, I said. That sounds correct.

*

A gap where the tooth was. The tongue keeps returning to it, this small architecture of loss, checking, checking. My father's crossword has a square he cannot fill. He leaves it blank. He goes back to it. This is also a kind of tongue, this returning.

*

TWELVE ACROSS: *forever*, or the abbreviation thereof.

*

I have gathered what I could. A baby tooth in my mother's jewelry box—she kept hers, she kept mine, she kept everyone's, that woman, a magpie of the body's discardings. I hold it now. It is smaller than a curse. It is the exact size of a curse.

*

To break the spell: the teeth, the burning, the impossible thanks. But the astrologer did not tell me that the spell and the grief are the same length. That you complete them at the same moment. That the moment is your own.

*

My father has finished the puzzle. Every square filled but one. He looks at it a long time. Then he writes, in the last white space, not a letter but a small mark, a thing that is not a word, a thing I cannot read from where I sit.

*

Thank you, I begin. To no one. To everyone. To the woman with the missing teeth in the mirror. Thank you, I say, and mean the first name on a list that has no end.

*

FINAL CLUE: what the living do (8 letters).

He fills it in. *Continue.*

*

He fills it in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem where the speaker follows an astrologer's visualization instructions but subverts them into an act of love and self-sacrifice at a crematorium.
counterfactuals.output:
**Instructions, Subverted**

The astrologer said: *Close your eyes.
Imagine a warm gold light above your crown.
Pull it down. Let it fill you. This is yours.*

I did. But I was not at home.
I was standing where the ovens hum their low
official hymn, where the attendant checks a form,
and I had come to gather what was mine—

so when the gold light gathered in my chest,
I did not keep it. *Draw it into every cell,*
she'd said, *until you glow, until you're whole.*
I let it pool, then pushed it out again,

sent it sliding under the steel door
to find you laid out cold and formal there,
your hands arranged by strangers, your good coat
buttoned to the throat you never buttoned once.

*Now feel the light protect you,* said the voice
still murmuring in the earbud I'd forgotten.
But I peeled the light from off my own bare shoulders
the way you'd peel a blanket for a child

and laid it over you. *This warmth is yours,*
the astrologer insisted. No. It's spent.
I gave the gold away. I kept the flame
that isn't metaphor—the real one, rising—

and when they say the body will not feel it,
I don't believe them. I have practiced this:
to close my eyes and stand inside the burning
so you would not go into it alone,

to take the visualization's promise—
*you deserve to hold the light, to be made new*—
and break it open like a loaf, and hand
every last warm piece across to you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal, melancholic prose poem about returning from the dead, wandering ruins, and a chainsaw-cutting curse ritual involving green boots.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Returning

I came back wearing the color of drowned wheat, and no one had left the lights on.

The ruins knew me by my absence—the way a mouth knows the socket of a pulled tooth. I walked the streets I had been buried beneath, and the pavement remembered my weight, sighed it back up through cracks where the dandelions had gone gray as ash and forgotten how to close at night.

*You were dead,* said the wind, not unkindly.

Yes. I had been very good at it.

Here is what death teaches: nothing. It is a long room with the furniture removed. It is the space after a name is spoken, when the name is you, and no one answers because you are the one who used to.

---

In the square where the fountain had choked on its own stone tongue, I found the green boots.

They stood alone, as if someone had stepped out of the world and left only their standing behind. Rubber the shade of pond-scum, of envy, of the going-under light. I did not put them on. Some inheritances are not for the wearing.

A woman was there—or the idea of a woman, thinning at the edges like breath on cold glass. She held the chainsaw the way a priest holds an argument with God.

*To cut a curse,* she told me, *you must find the thread that ties the dead to the coming-back. Then you sever it, and the sound is terrible, and the sound is mercy.*

She pulled the cord.

---

The chainsaw screamed the scream I had not been permitted in the grave. It ate the air. It ate the quiet. It carved through the invisible cord that ran from my sternum down into the earth, into the green boots, into the standing-place of everyone who ever left without leaving.

And I understood: the boots were mine. Had always been mine. I had died in them, green as spring, green as the last stupid hope, and they had stayed above ground doing my walking while I lay still.

The blade met rubber. Sparks the color of forsythia. A smell like the first day of a season that would not come.

---

When it was done, the woman was gone, and the boots were gone, and the ruins had begun—very slowly, the way forgiveness begins—to green.

I stood in my bare feet on the warming stone.

Not alive. Not dead. Only *here,* which is the hardest country of all, and the one they never tell you how to enter.

Somewhere, far off, a chainsaw idled down to nothing, satisfied.

I took a step.

The ground held me.

For now, the ground held me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary collage-style poem set in a decaying Oklahoma jazz neighborhood, mixing personal loss with a self-help magic spell about severing ties to someone.
counterfactuals.output:
**Severance Spell, Deep Deuce, Repeated**

*First, gather what the flood left:*
one shoe, a church program, the trumpet
your grandfather pawned in '68
and never walked back to claim.

Second Street sags into itself.
The brick façades wear their old names
like the faces of the drowned—
*Aldridge, Slaughter, the Ruby.*

*Take salt. Draw a line. Do not cross it.*

I keep meaning to tell you
the piano bar burned down
the year my mother stopped calling.
Somewhere a needle drops
into the groove of a record
no one owns anymore.

*Say his name once. Then bury the syllables
under the porch where the cats give birth.*

The magazine promised
*Ten Ways to Cut the Cord Forever*—
step four was *breathe*,
step six was *forgive the thief
of your own quiet.*

Weeds inherit the lot.
A saxophone, if you listen,
is only wind moving through
a thing that used to hold a song.

*Third: light the match. Watch how the paper
curls like a hand releasing.*

I severed you the way a city
severs its own heart—
by paving over it,
by calling it *renewal,*
by pretending
the music was never here.

But the ghosts still swing.
But the roots still crack the sidewalk.

*Fourth, and last:
what you release
will teach you what you were.*

Somewhere on Second Street
a door I loved stands open
onto nothing,
and I walk through it,
finally,
alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
